    "id": "01_intro_what_is_recurrence",
    "narration": "Imagine you're searching for a name in a phone book with one thousand pages. Rather than checking every page, you open to the middle, decide which half contains the name, discard the other half, and repeat. After just ten halvings, you're done — that's the power of halving. The question of precisely how many steps that process takes is what a recurrence relation answers. A recurrence relation is an equation that expresses an algorithm's runtime on a problem of size n in terms of its runtime on a smaller input — for our phone book search, that's T of n equals T of n over two, plus one step for the single comparison at each level.",
    "focusTarget": "#intro-what-is"
  },
  {
    "id": "02_intro_why_care",
    "narration": "Here is why this matters: a recurrence relation lets us predict an algorithm's scaling behavior before writing a single line of production code. Solving the relation gives us the Big-O complexity — the mathematical shape of how runtime grows as input size grows. The answers span a dramatic range, from O of log n for efficient divide-and-conquer, all the way to O of 2 to the n for naive recursive approaches. That gap is not subtle — at modest input sizes, it is literally the difference between finishing in milliseconds and never finishing at all. Knowing which category your algorithm falls into, and knowing it analytically rather than empirically, is one of the most powerful skills in computer science.",
    "focusTarget": "#intro-why-care"
  },
  {
    "id": "03_intro_tool_modules",
    "narration": "We have three complementary methods for solving recurrences, and each one offers a different lens on the same problem. The recursion tree method makes the solution visual — we draw every subproblem as a node, every recursive call as a branch, and then read the complexity directly off the structure of the tree. The Master Theorem is a formula shortcut that solves an entire family of divide-and-conquer recurrences almost instantly, once you learn to recognize the pattern. The substitution method is how we prove our answers rigorously, using mathematical induction to confirm that a proposed solution is exactly correct. Think of the three methods as building intuition, applying a shortcut, and then establishing certainty.",
    "focusTarget": "#intro-how-to-use"
  }
]

    "narration": "Welcome to the world of approximation algorithms!   }

    "id": "01_intro_what_is_recurrence",
    "narration": "Imagine you're searching for a name in a phone book with one thousand pages. Rather than checking every page, you open to the middle, decide which half contains the name, discard the other half, and repeat. After just ten halvings, you're done — that's the power of halving. The question of precisely how many steps that process takes is what a recurrence relation answers. A recurrence relation is an equation that expresses an algorithm's runtime on a problem of size n in terms of its runtime on a smaller input — for our phone book search, that's T of n equals T of n over two, plus one step for the single comparison at each level.",
    "focusTarget": "#intro-what-is"
  },
  {
    "id": "02_intro_why_care",
    "narration": "Here is why this matters: a recurrence relation lets us predict an algorithm's scaling behavior before writing a single line of production code. Solving the relation gives us the Big-O complexity — the mathematical shape of how runtime grows as input size grows. The answers span a dramatic range, from O of log n for efficient divide-and-conquer, all the way to O of 2 to the n for naive recursive approaches. That gap is not subtle — at modest input sizes, it is literally the difference between finishing in milliseconds and never finishing at all. Knowing which category your algorithm falls into, and knowing it analytically rather than empirically, is one of the most powerful skills in computer science.",
    "focusTarget": "#intro-why-care"
  },
  {
    "id": "03_intro_tool_modules",
    "narration": "We have three complementary methods for solving recurrences, and each one offers a different lens on the same problem. The recursion tree method makes the solution visual — we draw every subproblem as a node, every recursive call as a branch, and then read the complexity directly off the structure of the tree. The Master Theorem is a formula shortcut that solves an entire family of divide-and-conquer recurrences almost instantly, once you learn to recognize the pattern. The substitution method is how we prove our answers rigorously, using mathematical induction to confirm that a proposed solution is exactly correct. Think of the three methods as building intuition, applying a shortcut, and then establishing certainty.",
    "focusTarget": "#intro-how-to-use"
  },
  {
    "id": "04_intro_learning_path",
    "narration": "We will follow a five-algorithm progression, carefully ordered from simplest to most revealing. Binary Search sets the baseline — one subproblem per call, a logarithmic answer. Merge Sort introduces branching, where two recursive calls compound the work to O of n log n. Naive Fibonacci is the cautionary tale: overlapping subproblems cause exponential blowup, and the recurrence makes that visible before you ever run the code. Memoized Fibonacci demonstrates how eliminating redundant computation collapses the runtime from exponential to linear in a single conceptual move. Tower of Hanoi closes the progression — an elegantly simple recurrence with an answer that is provably, unavoidably exponential.",

Push to n equals one hundred, and the exponential algorithm requires a number with thirty digits — more operations than there are atoms in a human body. This is not a rounding error, not a constant factor, not something a faster processor fixes.     "narration": "Imagine you're searching for a name in a phone book with one thousand pages. Rather than checking every page, you open to the middle, decide which half contains the name, discard the other half, and repeat. After just ten halvings, you're done — that's the power of halving. The question of precisely how many steps that process takes is what a recurrence relation answers. A recurrence relation is an equation that expresses an algorithm's runtime on a problem of size n in terms of its runtime on a smaller input — for our phone book search, that's T of n equals T of n over two, plus one step for the single comparison at each level.",

    "narration": "Here is why this matters: a recurrence relation lets us predict an algorithm's scaling behavior before writing a single line of production code. The answers span a dramatic range, from O of log n for efficient divide-and-conquer, all the way to O of 2 to the n for naive recursive approaches. That gap is not subtle — at modest input sizes, it is literally the difference between finishing in milliseconds and never finishing at all. The substitution method is how we prove our answers rigorously, using mathematical induction to confirm that a proposed solution is exactly correct.     "narration": "Imagine you're searching for a name in a phone book with one thousand pages. A recurrence relation is an equation that expresses an algorithm's runtime on a problem of size n in terms of its runtime on a smaller input — for our phone book search, that's T of n equals T of n over two, plus one step for the single comparison at each level.",

The answers span a dramatic range, from O of log n for efficient divide-and-conquer, all the way to O of 2 to the n for naive recursive approaches. That gap is not subtle — at modest input sizes, it is literally the difference between finishing in milliseconds and never finishing at all. The Master Theorem is a formula shortcut that solves an entire family of divide-and-conquer recurrences almost instantly, once you learn to recognize the pattern.     "id": "01_intro_what_is_recurrence",
    "narration": "Imagine you're searching for a name in a phone book with one thousand pages. Rather than checking every page, you open to the middle, decide which half contains the name, discard the other half, and repeat. After just ten halvings, you're done — that's the power of halving. The question of precisely how many steps that process takes is what a recurrence relation answers. A recurrence relation is an equation that expresses an algorithm's runtime on a problem of size n in terms of its runtime on a smaller input — for our phone book search, that's T of n equals T of n over two, plus one step for the single comparison at each level.",

    "id": "02_intro_why_care",
    "narration": "Here is why this matters: a recurrence relation lets us predict an algorithm's scaling behavior before writing a single line of production code. Solving the relation gives us the Big-O complexity — the mathematical shape of how runtime grows as input size grows. The answers span a dramatic range, from O of log n for efficient divide-and-conquer, all the way to O of 2 to the n for naive recursive approaches. That gap is not subtle — at modest input sizes, it is literally the difference between finishing in milliseconds and never finishing at all. The Master Theorem is a formula shortcut that solves an entire family of divide-and-conquer recurrences almost instantly, once you learn to recognize the pattern. The substitution method is how we prove our answers rigorously, using mathematical induction to confirm that a proposed solution is exactly correct.     "narration": "Imagine you're searching for a name in a phone book with one thousand pages. Rather than checking every page, you open to the middle, decide which half contains the name, discard the other half, and repeat. After just ten halvings, you're done — that's the power of halving. The question of precisely how many steps that process takes is what a recurrence relation answers. A recurrence relation is an equation that expresses an algorithm's runtime on a problem of size n in terms of its runtime on a smaller input — for our phone book search, that's T of n equals T of n over two, plus one step for the single comparison at each level.",

The answers span a dramatic range, from O of log n for efficient divide-and-conquer, all the way to O of 2 to the n for naive recursive approaches. That gap is not subtle — at modest input sizes, it is literally the difference between finishing in milliseconds and never finishing at all.
